newsitem.title: USA: U.S. trade gap widens by 17.0 percent in May.
newsitem.headline: U.S. trade gap widens by 17.0 percent in May.

text.p: The U.S. trade deficit soared by 17.0 percent to $10.23 billion in May as foreign imports hit an all-time record high, the government reported on Friday.

High levels of consumer confidence and the dollar's buying power overseas were a driving force behind the seventh straight monthly gain in imports. The shortfall was the widest since January and bigger than forecast.
"U.S. economic growth continues to be robust even though it is slowing down," said Sung Won Sohn, chief economist at Norwest Corp. in Minneapolis. "We are sucking up a lot of imports from overseas."

Imports continued their steady upward march, rising by a modest 1.0 percent in May to $87.5 billion, led by demand for foreign-made airplanes, cars and industrial supplies and materials like crude oil, the Commerce Department said.
At the same time, May exports fell 0.8 percent to $77.2 billion, reflecting a drop in exports of capital goods, such as telecommunications equipment.
"We are starting to see a slowdown in the export mini-boom," said Michael Niemira, economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd. in New York.

The resulting May trade deficit exceeded the expectations of Wall Street analysts, who were looking for a $9.18 billion May trade gap. The April trade gap was revised upward to $8.75 billion from the $8.36 billion originally reported.
The U.S. trade imbalance with China widened by 9.1 percent in May to $3.76 billion from $3.45 billion in April. The gap was the highest since since the October 1996 deficit of $4.9 billion.
The deficit with China surpassed that of Japan, only the third time in history that has happened, the department noted.
But the politically sensitive deficit with Japan was the lowest since last June. The gap shrank by 25 percent to $3.63 billion from $4.84 billion in April.

The May trade data showed the U.S. trade gaps with Canada and Mexico widening, with the news coming just days after the Clinton administration hailed the benefits of the North American Free Trade Agreement.
The pact, which went into effect at the beginning of 1994, links the United States, Canada and Mexico in a trading bloc.

The U.S. trade deficit with Mexico swelled by 21.7 percent to a record $1.7 billion from $1.4 billion in April. In trade with Canada, the deficit more than doubled, rising 104.1 percent to $1.74 billion in May.
Imports from Canada of $14.5 billion in May were the highest on record with any country, the department said.

Analysts noted that gains in imports of capital goods typically mean that businesses are gearing up for future activity, suggesting the economy may firm up later this year following an expected slowdown in second-quarter growth.

"Any time you see imports picking up it's a good proxy for how strong the underlying demand is," said Anthony Chan, chief economsit at Banc One Investment Advisors Corp. in Columbus, Ohio. "It's not consistent with the notion that in the second half of the year the economy is going to tank."
The report also showed that the United States had a deficit with Western Europe of $1.29 billion after recording a $486 million deficit in April.
The merchandise trade gap rose 9.8 percent in May to $17.0 billion, while the services surplus rose 0.5 percent to $6.81 billion, the department said.
Foreign sales of civilian aircraft rose to $2.61 billion from $2.40 billion in April.
The cost of imported crude oil rose in May to $4.6 billion as the price per barrel dropped to $17 from $17.17 in April and $18.72 in March.
